easy.text: What is a linked list, as a data structure?

options.text: A sequence of nodes where each node holds data and a pointer to the next node
options.feedback: Correct -- a linked list chains nodes together using pointers rather than storing elements side by side.

options.text: A single number stored in one memory location
options.feedback: A linked list is a whole structure of connected nodes, not a single stored number.

options.text: A fixed grid of rows and columns used to store a table
options.feedback: A grid of rows and columns describes something more like a 2D array or table, not a linked list.

options.text: A block of code that repeats a set of instructions
options.feedback: That describes a loop, not a data structure made of connected nodes.

medium.text: What is a key structural difference between a linked list and an array?

options.text: A linked list's nodes are connected by pointers and don't need to sit in contiguous memory, unlike an array
options.feedback: Correct -- this is the defining structural difference between the two.

options.text: A linked list must always be stored in sorted order, while an array can never be sorted
options.feedback: Neither structure is required to be sorted or forbidden from being sorted -- that's not the real distinction.

options.text: A linked list can only hold numbers, while an array can hold any data type
options.feedback: Both structures can hold many different data types -- storage layout, not allowed content, is the real distinction.

options.text: A linked list and an array are simply two names for the same underlying storage method
options.feedback: They use genuinely different memory layouts -- contiguous versus scattered-and-linked.

hard.text: Why can inserting a new element at the very front of a linked list be done in constant time, O(1), while doing the same in an array typically takes O(n) time?

options.text: Inserting at the front of a linked list only requires updating a couple of pointers, whereas an array must shift every existing element over by one position
options.feedback: Correct -- the linked list avoids the shifting cost entirely because nothing needs to move, only pointers change.

options.text: Because linked lists are always stored on faster physical memory chips than arrays
options.feedback: Both structures live in the same ordinary memory -- speed differences come from the algorithm, not different hardware.

options.text: Because arrays are not allowed to have new elements added to them after creation
options.feedback: Elements can be added to arrays -- it's just that doing so at the front is costly, not impossible.

options.text: Because a linked list automatically keeps itself sorted whenever a new element is added
options.feedback: Linked lists don't auto-sort -- the speed advantage comes from pointer updates, not ordering.

easy.easy: Think about a chain of connected pieces, where each piece knows where the next one is.
easy.medium: Each element in this structure is called a node, and every node holds a link pointing to the next node.
easy.hard: The structure is defined by nodes connected via pointers, rather than being packed into one contiguous block of memory.

medium.easy: Think about how the elements sit in memory -- packed right next to each other, or scattered and connected by links?
medium.medium: One structure keeps its elements in one continuous block; the other scatters nodes and connects them with pointers.
medium.hard: Because its nodes are connected via pointers rather than sitting in contiguous memory, this structure's elements don't need to be right next to each other.

hard.easy: Adding to the front of one of these structures just rewires a couple of connections, without touching anything else.
hard.medium: One operation only needs to update a couple of pointers; the other has to physically shift every remaining element over by one spot.
hard.hard: The constant-time insertion comes from only updating the head pointer and the new node's own pointer -- no shifting of other elements required.

easy.text: What makes a 'doubly' linked list different from a standard (singly) linked list?

options.text: Each node holds a pointer to both the next node AND the previous node
options.feedback: Correct -- the 'doubly' in the name refers to links running in both directions.

options.text: Each node stores its data value written twice
options.feedback: The 'doubly' refers to pointer directions, not the data being duplicated.

options.text: It contains exactly double the number of nodes as a singly linked list
options.feedback: Node count isn't fixed by the type of list -- the difference is about pointer direction, not quantity.

options.text: It can only be used to store even numbers
options.feedback: A doubly linked list can store any kind of data -- this has nothing to do with even numbers.

medium.text: What is a practical advantage a doubly linked list has over a singly linked list?

options.text: It allows traversal in both the forward and backward directions
options.feedback: Correct -- because each node knows its previous node too, you can walk the list in reverse without extra work.

options.text: It uses less memory per node than a singly linked list
options.feedback: A doubly linked list actually uses MORE memory per node, since it stores an extra backward pointer.

options.text: It guarantees the data stays sorted automatically
options.feedback: Neither list type sorts itself automatically -- the advantage is about traversal direction, not ordering.

options.text: It removes the need for a head pointer to the first node
options.feedback: A doubly linked list still needs a reference to its starting node, just like a singly linked list.

hard.text: What is a notable tradeoff of using a doubly linked list instead of a singly linked list?

options.text: Each node requires extra memory for the additional backward pointer, and that pointer must be kept updated during insertions and deletions
options.feedback: Correct -- the backward-traversal benefit comes at the cost of extra memory and extra pointer bookkeeping on every modification.

options.text: It becomes impossible to insert new nodes once the list has been created
options.feedback: Insertion is still fully possible in a doubly linked list -- it just requires updating one extra pointer per operation.

options.text: It can no longer store more than a fixed maximum number of elements
options.feedback: There's no such fixed cap introduced by adding backward pointers -- the tradeoff is memory and bookkeeping overhead, not a size limit.

options.text: Searching for an element becomes an O(1) constant-time operation
options.feedback: Searching still requires walking node by node, so it remains an O(n) operation, same as in a singly linked list.

easy.easy: The defining feature is a second pointer per node, aimed at the previous node in the sequence.
easy.medium: Each link in the chain points to its neighbor on both sides, not just the one ahead of it.
easy.hard: Picture a chain where you can walk not just forward, but also backward.

medium.easy: Because each node also references its previous neighbor, you can walk the sequence backward as easily as forward.
medium.medium: This benefit is about which directions you can travel through the structure, not about memory usage or automatic sorting.
medium.hard: Think about which direction you're able to walk through the sequence.

hard.easy: Every node now carries a second pointer that must be updated on every insertion or deletion, at the cost of additional memory per node.
hard.medium: The cost shows up as more memory per node and more pointers to keep in sync, not as a hard limit on size or search speed.
hard.hard: Extra convenience for traversal comes with an extra cost that has to be paid on every node.

easy.text: In a binary tree, what is the maximum number of children a single node can have?

options.text: Two
options.feedback: Correct -- 'binary' refers to each node having at most two children, typically called left and right.

options.text: One
options.feedback: A binary tree node can have up to two children, not just one.

options.text: Four
options.feedback: Four children would describe a different kind of tree -- a binary tree caps each node at two children.

options.text: An unlimited number
options.feedback: An unlimited number of children isn't allowed in a binary tree -- that's the defining limit of two.

medium.text: In binary tree terminology, what is a 'leaf' node?

options.text: A node that has no children
options.feedback: Correct -- leaf nodes sit at the ends of the tree's branches, with nothing growing below them.

options.text: The topmost node in the entire tree
options.feedback: The topmost node is called the 'root', not a 'leaf'.

options.text: Any node that has exactly two children
options.feedback: A node with two children is often called a 'full' or 'internal' node -- a leaf specifically has zero children.

options.text: A node that stores a decimal number instead of an integer
options.feedback: The term 'leaf' describes a node's position in the tree structure, not the data type it stores.

hard.text: What distinguishes a 'balanced' binary tree from an unbalanced one?

options.text: In a balanced tree, the heights of the left and right subtrees of every node differ by no more than a small, bounded amount
options.feedback: Correct -- balance keeps the tree's height close to logarithmic in the number of nodes, keeping operations fast.

options.text: A balanced tree must contain an equal number of leaf nodes and internal nodes
options.feedback: Balance is about subtree HEIGHT being kept even, not about leaf and internal node counts matching.

options.text: A balanced tree is one where every node holds the exact same value
options.feedback: Nodes holding identical values isn't what 'balanced' refers to -- it's about the tree's shape and height.

options.text: An unbalanced tree is simply one that has more than one root node
options.feedback: A tree, balanced or not, has exactly one root -- 'unbalanced' describes uneven subtree heights, not multiple roots.

easy.hard: The name of this structure hints at a specific small number as the cap on children per node.
easy.medium: The word 'binary' itself signals the maximum branching factor allowed per node here.
easy.easy: Each node can have at most a left child and a right child -- and no more than that.

medium.hard: Think about which nodes sit at the very ends of the tree's branches, with nothing beneath them.
medium.medium: This term names a node at the bottom of a branch -- one that doesn't have anything branching further beneath it.
medium.easy: This is a node with zero children -- contrast that with the 'root' at the top or a 'full' node with two children.

hard.hard: Think about how evenly the tree's branches grow on each side of every node.
hard.medium: This property is about keeping the left and right subtree heights close to each other at every node, not about counting nodes or matching values.
hard.easy: Bounding how much the left and right subtree heights can differ at every node is exactly what keeps operations fast on this kind of tree.

easy.text: What ordering rule defines a binary search tree?

options.text: For every node, all values in its left subtree are smaller, and all values in its right subtree are larger
options.feedback: Correct -- this ordering rule is what makes searching in the tree efficient.

options.text: Every node must hold a value larger than all other nodes in the tree
options.feedback: Only the single largest value can satisfy that, not every node -- the rule applies relative to each node's own subtrees.

options.text: Nodes are arranged in the exact order they were originally typed into a list
options.feedback: Insertion order isn't what defines the structure -- the value-based left/right ordering rule is what matters.

options.text: All nodes at the same depth must hold identical values
options.feedback: Nodes don't need matching values at any depth -- ordering is based on comparing values via the left/right rule.

medium.text: Why does searching for a value in a well-balanced binary search tree tend to be much faster than searching an unsorted list of the same size?

options.text: At each step, comparing against a node lets you eliminate an entire subtree, roughly halving the remaining search space
options.feedback: Correct -- this halving behavior is what gives balanced binary search trees their logarithmic search time.

options.text: Because binary search trees store their data using less memory than a list does
options.feedback: Memory usage per element isn't what drives the search speed advantage -- it's the ability to skip entire subtrees.

options.text: Because every node in a binary search tree is checked at the exact same time in parallel
options.feedback: Searching a tree is typically done step by step, not by checking every node simultaneously.

options.text: Because binary search trees never contain duplicate values
options.feedback: Whether duplicates are allowed isn't what makes searches fast -- the ordering rule that lets you skip subtrees is.

hard.text: What happens to a binary search tree's search efficiency if values are inserted in already-sorted order (e.g., 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, ...)?

options.text: The tree degenerates into something resembling a single chain of nodes, making search take O(n) time instead of O(log n)
options.feedback: Correct -- without rebalancing, sorted-order insertion produces a lopsided tree that loses the usual logarithmic search speed.

options.text: The tree automatically rebalances itself to stay efficient, regardless of insertion order
options.feedback: A plain binary search tree does not automatically rebalance -- that behavior specifically requires a self-balancing variant.

options.text: Search efficiency is completely unaffected by the order values are inserted in
options.feedback: Insertion order matters a great deal for a plain binary search tree's shape and resulting search speed.

options.text: The tree simply refuses to insert any values that arrive in sorted order
options.feedback: A binary search tree will still accept sorted-order insertions -- it just ends up shaped inefficiently as a result.

easy.hard: Compare a value against a node: smaller values go one direction, larger values go the other.
easy.medium: At every node, one whole side of the tree holds only smaller values, and the other side holds only larger ones.
easy.easy: Every node's left branch holds only smaller values than it, and its right branch holds only larger ones.

medium.hard: Each comparison lets you throw away a big chunk of the remaining nodes at once.
medium.medium: Because one comparison rules out an entire subtree, the amount of data left to search shrinks quickly with each step.
medium.easy: This step-by-step process of cutting away half of what's left to search, again and again, is what makes lookups so fast.

hard.hard: Think about what shape the tree ends up taking if every new value is always bigger than the last one added.
hard.medium: Without any rebalancing step, inserting already-sorted values tends to produce a long, lopsided shape rather than a bushy one.
hard.easy: The tree can end up shaped almost like a straight line of nodes, which erases the usual speed advantage over a plain list.

easy.text: What does it mean to 'traverse' a tree data structure?

options.text: To visit every node in the tree, following some defined order
options.feedback: Correct -- traversal is the process of systematically visiting each node.

options.text: To permanently delete every node in the tree
options.feedback: Traversal is about visiting nodes, not deleting them.

options.text: To copy the tree's nodes into a completely different data structure called a stack
options.feedback: A stack might be used as a tool during traversal, but traversal itself just means visiting nodes in order, not converting the tree.

options.text: To count only the leaf nodes and ignore the rest
options.feedback: Traversal generally visits ALL relevant nodes, not just the leaves.

medium.text: In an 'in-order' traversal of a binary search tree, in what order are the nodes visited?

options.text: Left subtree, then the current node, then the right subtree
options.feedback: Correct -- for a binary search tree, this specific order happens to visit nodes in ascending sorted order.

options.text: Current node, then left subtree, then right subtree
options.feedback: That visiting order describes a 'pre-order' traversal, not an 'in-order' one.

options.text: Left subtree, then right subtree, then the current node
options.feedback: That visiting order describes a 'post-order' traversal, not an 'in-order' one.

options.text: Only the root node, skipping every other node entirely
options.feedback: In-order traversal visits every node in the tree, not just the root.

hard.text: Why does an in-order traversal of a valid binary search tree always produce its values in ascending sorted order?

options.text: Because at every node, the traversal fully visits the smaller left subtree before the node itself, and the node before the larger right subtree, mirroring the tree's own ordering rule
options.feedback: Correct -- the left-node-right visiting pattern lines up exactly with the tree's own smaller-left, larger-right structure.

options.text: Because binary search trees secretly store their values in an array behind the scenes
options.feedback: A binary search tree is made of linked nodes, not a hidden array -- the sorted output comes from the traversal order matching the tree's structure.

options.text: Because the traversal randomly shuffles values until they happen to land in order
options.feedback: The traversal follows a fixed, deterministic order -- there's no randomness or shuffling involved.

options.text: Because every binary search tree is required to already be a straight line of nodes
options.feedback: Binary search trees can take many shapes, not just a straight line -- the sorted result comes from the traversal order, not from the tree being a chain.

easy.easy: Think of it as a systematic walk through the tree, stopping at each node along the way.
easy.medium: This is the general process of visiting every node in the tree according to some chosen order.
easy.hard: The word describes visiting, not deleting, copying, or filtering down to only certain nodes.

medium.hard: This order visits one side, then the middle, then the other side.
medium.medium: The pattern is: left side first, then the current node itself, then the right side.
medium.easy: Picture visiting everything on the left branch first, then the node itself, then everything on the right branch -- in that exact order.

hard.hard: Notice how the traversal's own left-then-node-then-right pattern lines up with how the tree was built.
hard.medium: Because smaller values always sit to the left and larger ones to the right at every node, visiting left-node-right naturally outputs values from smallest to largest.
hard.easy: The match between the tree's own smaller-left/larger-right ordering rule and the traversal's left-node-right visiting pattern is exactly why the output comes out sorted.

easy.text: In computer science, what is a graph made up of?

options.text: A set of nodes (vertices) connected by edges
options.feedback: Correct -- a graph is fundamentally a collection of vertices linked together by edges.

options.text: A single continuous line drawn on a chart to show trends over time
options.feedback: That describes a line chart used for visualizing data, not the graph data structure used in computer science.

options.text: A list of numbers sorted from smallest to largest
options.feedback: A sorted list of numbers doesn't involve vertices and edges -- that's not what a graph data structure is.

options.text: A fixed grid of exactly 8 rows and 8 columns
options.feedback: A graph's shape isn't fixed to any particular grid size -- it's defined by its vertices and edges instead.

medium.text: What distinguishes a 'directed' graph from an 'undirected' graph?

options.text: In a directed graph, each edge points from one vertex to another in a specific direction, while undirected edges can be traveled either way
options.feedback: Correct -- direction on an edge means the connection only goes one way, unlike a two-way undirected edge.

options.text: A directed graph must always contain more vertices than an undirected graph
options.feedback: Vertex count has nothing to do with the directed/undirected distinction -- it's about whether edges have a direction.

options.text: An undirected graph cannot contain any cycles, while a directed graph always must
options.feedback: Both directed and undirected graphs can contain cycles or be free of them -- that's not the defining difference.

options.text: A directed graph is only used for storing text data, while undirected graphs store numbers
options.feedback: The type of data stored isn't related to whether a graph is directed -- the distinction is about edge direction.

hard.text: What is a key structural difference between a 'tree' and a general graph?

options.text: A tree is a specific kind of graph that is connected and contains no cycles, while a general graph can have cycles and disconnected parts
options.feedback: Correct -- every tree is technically a graph, but not every graph qualifies as a tree, precisely because of the no-cycles, fully-connected requirement.

options.text: A tree can only have one single vertex in total, while a graph can have many
options.feedback: A tree can have many vertices, just like a graph -- the real distinction is about cycles and connectivity.

options.text: A graph must always be drawn with straight lines, while a tree can use curved lines
options.feedback: How something is visually drawn isn't a structural property -- the actual distinction concerns cycles and connectivity.

options.text: A tree allows an edge to connect a vertex to itself, while a graph never allows that
options.feedback: This reverses the general rule -- graphs, not trees, are the ones that can permit self-loops depending on the graph type.

easy.hard: Picture dots connected by lines -- that's the basic shape of this structure.
easy.medium: This structure is built from two ingredients: points, and the connections drawn between them.
easy.easy: Formally, this is a set of points (vertices) together with a set of connections (edges) linking pairs of them.

medium.hard: Consider whether following a connection from one point to another also guarantees you could follow it back the other way.
medium.medium: One type's connections work like a one-way street; the other type's connections work like a two-way street.
medium.easy: The key is whether each edge has an arrow-like direction attached to it, restricting travel to one way, or allows travel both ways.

hard.hard: One of these structures is really just a special, more restricted case of the other.
hard.medium: The special case adds two extra requirements on top of being a graph -- something about how its pieces stay linked, and something about paths that loop back.
hard.easy: Staying connected with zero loops that circle back on themselves is exactly what turns a general graph into this more restricted structure.

easy.text: What is an 'adjacency list' used for in computer science?

options.text: Representing which vertices in a graph are connected to which other vertices
options.feedback: Correct -- an adjacency list stores, for each vertex, the other vertices it's directly connected to.

options.text: Sorting a list of numbers into ascending order
options.feedback: Sorting numbers is unrelated to representing connections between vertices in a graph.

options.text: Storing the login passwords for a website's users
options.feedback: An adjacency list is a way of representing graph connections, not a place to store passwords.

options.text: Keeping track of a program's variable names alphabetically
options.feedback: Alphabetizing variable names isn't related to representing which vertices connect to which.

medium.text: How does an 'adjacency matrix' represent a graph's connections?

options.text: As a grid where each cell indicates whether an edge exists between the corresponding pair of vertices
options.feedback: Correct -- rows and columns represent vertices, and each cell marks the presence or absence of a connecting edge.

options.text: As a single sorted list of all the vertex names, with no information about edges at all
options.feedback: An adjacency matrix specifically encodes edge connections in its grid, not just a bare list of vertex names.

options.text: As a chain of nodes where each node points only to the very next vertex added
options.feedback: That describes something closer to a linked list, not the row-and-column grid structure of an adjacency matrix.

options.text: As a single number representing the total count of vertices in the graph
options.feedback: A single count wouldn't capture which specific vertices connect to which -- that's what the full grid is for.

hard.text: For a graph with many vertices but relatively few edges (a 'sparse' graph), why is an adjacency list typically more memory-efficient than an adjacency matrix?

options.text: An adjacency list only stores space for edges that actually exist, while an adjacency matrix reserves space for every possible pair of vertices regardless of whether an edge connects them
options.feedback: Correct -- a matrix's size grows with the square of the vertex count, wasting space on pairs with no edge, while a list scales with the actual number of edges.

options.text: An adjacency matrix can only represent graphs with fewer than ten vertices
options.feedback: An adjacency matrix can represent graphs of any size -- the issue is wasted space for missing edges, not a hard vertex limit.

options.text: An adjacency list is incapable of representing directed graphs
options.feedback: Adjacency lists can represent directed graphs just fine -- efficiency for sparse graphs is the actual point of comparison here.

options.text: An adjacency matrix requires the graph's edges to all have the exact same weight
options.feedback: Adjacency matrices can store varying edge weights -- the memory tradeoff is about representing existing versus all-possible connections.

easy.hard: Picture describing a network of connections without drawing out every possible pair -- what's the minimal way to note who's linked to whom?
easy.medium: This structure stores, per vertex, a list of that vertex's direct neighbors.
easy.easy: It's a per-vertex list of directly connected neighbors, used to represent a graph's edges.

medium.hard: Picture a table where rows and columns are both labeled with the same set of points.
medium.medium: Each cell in this grid corresponds to one specific pair of vertices -- one from the row, one from the column -- and holds some kind of marker about that pair.
medium.easy: The grid's rows and columns both represent vertices, and each cell marks whether an edge connects that specific pair.

hard.hard: Think about what happens to a full grid's size when there are many points but few connections between them.
hard.medium: One representation's size depends only on how many connections there really are, while the other's size depends on how many points there are, connected or not.
hard.easy: A grid-based representation's size grows with vertices squared no matter how many edges exist, while a per-vertex list only grows with the edges that are truly there.

easy.text: What is the defining property of a 'min-heap'?

options.text: Every parent node's value is less than or equal to the values of its children
options.feedback: Correct -- this ordering rule guarantees the smallest value in the whole structure always sits at the root.

options.text: Every node in the heap must hold a negative number
options.feedback: A min-heap can store any comparable values, not just negative numbers -- the rule is about parent-child ordering.

options.text: The heap must contain exactly the same number of nodes at every level
options.feedback: A heap is generally kept 'complete' in a specific structural sense, but the defining ordering property is about parent-versus-children values.

options.text: Values must be stored in a chain, with each node pointing only to the previous one
options.feedback: That describes something closer to a linked list, not the parent-smaller-than-children rule that defines a min-heap.

medium.text: Why is a heap well-suited for efficiently retrieving the minimum (or maximum) value from a collection?

options.text: Because the ordering property guarantees the minimum (or maximum) value is always located at the root, retrievable in constant time
options.feedback: Correct -- you never need to search the whole structure just to find the current smallest or largest value.

options.text: Because a heap keeps all of its values in fully sorted order from smallest to largest at all times
options.feedback: A heap is only partially ordered -- only the parent-child relationship is guaranteed, not a fully sorted sequence.

options.text: Because a heap only ever stores a single value at any given time
options.feedback: A heap can hold many values simultaneously -- efficient min/max retrieval comes from the ordering rule, not from limiting size to one.

options.text: Because every value in a heap must be unique, with no duplicates permitted
options.feedback: Heaps can absolutely contain duplicate values -- the retrieval efficiency comes from the parent-child ordering rule, not uniqueness.

hard.text: Why does removing the root element from a heap and restoring its ordering property typically take O(log n) time rather than O(1) or O(n)?

options.text: Because after removal, a replacement value must be 'sifted down' level by level to restore the ordering property, and the number of levels in the heap grows logarithmically with the number of elements
options.feedback: Correct -- the sift-down operation only has to travel down the heap's height, which stays proportional to log n because the heap remains a balanced, complete structure.

options.text: Because the entire heap must be fully re-sorted from scratch after every single removal
options.feedback: A full re-sort would take longer than necessary -- only a sift-down along one path is required to restore the heap property.

options.text: Because removing the root requires searching every single node in the heap one at a time
options.feedback: There's no need to search every node -- restoring the property only follows a path down through the heap's levels.

options.text: Because a heap only allows removals to happen at fixed time intervals, not on demand
options.feedback: Removals happen on demand whenever requested -- the log n cost purely reflects the sift-down operation's path length.

easy.hard: Think about a rule comparing each 'parent' spot in the structure to its 'children' spots below it.
easy.medium: The rule says every parent must be no greater than (or, in the other variant, no less than) its own children.
easy.easy: In the 'min' version specifically, no parent is ever allowed to hold a bigger number than the values sitting right below it.

medium.hard: Think about which single spot in the structure is guaranteed to hold the smallest (or largest) value.
medium.medium: One particular position -- the very top of the structure -- is always guaranteed to hold the extreme value.
medium.easy: Because the structure's ordering rule always pins the smallest (or largest) value to that one top spot, you never have to search around for it.

hard.hard: After removing the top value, some value has to move down through the levels to fix the ordering rule again.
hard.medium: This fix-up step travels downward one level at a time, and the number of levels available is what limits how long it takes.
hard.easy: The sifting-down process only ever has to move through the heap's height, and that height grows in proportion to the log of how many elements are stored.

easy.text: What makes a 'priority queue' different from a regular queue?

options.text: Each element has an associated priority, and elements with higher priority are served before elements with lower priority, regardless of arrival order
options.feedback: Correct -- a priority queue serves based on priority value, not strictly on first-come-first-served order.

options.text: A priority queue can only ever hold a single element at any given time
options.feedback: A priority queue can hold many elements at once -- the difference is about the ORDER they get served in.

options.text: A priority queue always serves elements in the exact order they arrived, just like a regular queue
options.feedback: That describes ordinary first-in-first-out behavior -- a priority queue instead serves based on priority, not arrival order.

options.text: A priority queue is simply another name for a stack
options.feedback: A stack serves the most recently added element first (last-in-first-out) -- a priority queue serves based on priority value instead.

medium.text: Which underlying data structure is commonly used to efficiently implement a priority queue?

options.text: A heap
options.feedback: Correct -- a heap's ordering property makes it efficient to repeatedly retrieve and remove the highest (or lowest) priority element.

options.text: A simple unordered list with no particular structure
options.feedback: An unordered list would require scanning every element just to find the highest priority one, making it far less efficient than a heap-based implementation.

options.text: A single standalone variable holding one value
options.feedback: A single variable can't hold a whole collection of prioritized elements -- an actual data structure like a heap is needed.

options.text: A fixed-size grid with a fixed number of rows and columns
options.feedback: A fixed grid isn't the typical efficient backing structure for a priority queue -- a heap is the standard choice.

hard.text: In a real-world scenario like an operating system's task scheduler, why might a priority queue be preferred over a plain first-in-first-out queue?

options.text: It lets more urgent or important tasks be handled before less urgent ones, even if those less urgent tasks arrived earlier
options.feedback: Correct -- this is exactly the kind of scenario where serving strictly by arrival order would be undesirable, since urgency should matter more than arrival time.

options.text: Because a plain first-in-first-out queue is physically incapable of storing more than a few tasks
options.feedback: A plain queue can store as many tasks as memory allows -- the real benefit of a priority queue is ordering by importance, not raw storage capacity.

options.text: Because tasks in a priority queue are guaranteed to complete instantly regardless of their actual workload
options.feedback: A priority queue affects the ORDER tasks are handled in -- it doesn't change how long any individual task actually takes to complete.

options.text: Because a priority queue removes the need for the operating system to track tasks at all
options.feedback: Tasks still need to be tracked in a priority queue -- it simply tracks and serves them according to priority rather than arrival time.

easy.hard: Each item waiting in line here carries an extra piece of information: how important or urgent it is.
easy.medium: Think about a waiting line where some people get called up sooner because of how urgent their situation is, not just who arrived first.
easy.easy: Elements marked as higher priority jump ahead of lower-priority elements, even ones that arrived earlier.

medium.hard: Think back to a structure where the most extreme (highest or lowest) value always sits in one easy-to-reach spot.
medium.medium: This structure's built-in ordering rule makes it efficient to repeatedly grab the top-priority item.
medium.easy: Its parent-versus-children ordering rule is exactly why it's the go-to structure for backing a priority-based queue.

hard.hard: Think about a case where handling things strictly in arrival order would clearly be the wrong approach.
hard.medium: Urgency, not arrival time, decides who gets handled next in this kind of scenario.
hard.easy: Serving by importance rather than strictly by arrival time lets more critical work jump ahead of less critical work that arrived earlier.

easy.text: What is a 'trie' (prefix tree) primarily used to store efficiently?

options.text: A set of strings, organized so that strings sharing a common prefix share the same path in the tree
options.feedback: Correct -- a trie is specifically built around organizing text by shared prefixes.

options.text: A single large image file
options.feedback: A trie is built for organizing text-like data by shared prefixes, not for storing image files.

options.text: A fixed collection of exactly two numeric values
options.feedback: A trie's purpose is prefix-based string storage, not holding a small fixed number of numeric values.

options.text: An unordered pile of unrelated random values with no shared structure
options.feedback: A trie specifically organizes strings around SHARED prefixes -- it isn't just an unordered pile of unrelated values.

medium.text: Why are tries especially useful for implementing features like autocomplete?

options.text: Because all strings sharing a given prefix are grouped along the same path, making it fast to find every word starting with that prefix
options.feedback: Correct -- once you've walked down to a given prefix's node, everything below it in the trie shares that same starting text.

options.text: Because a trie stores every possible word in the English language by default, with no data entry required
options.feedback: A trie only contains whatever strings have actually been inserted into it -- it doesn't come pre-loaded with a full language's vocabulary.

options.text: Because a trie can only ever store a single word at a time
options.feedback: A trie is built to store many words at once, organized by shared prefixes -- that's precisely what makes it useful for autocomplete.

options.text: Because a trie automatically corrects any spelling mistakes in a given search term
options.feedback: A trie helps find matches quickly based on prefixes -- automatic spelling correction is a separate feature, not an inherent trie property.

hard.text: What is a common space-related tradeoff of using a trie to store a large set of strings, compared to storing them in a simple list?

options.text: A trie can use considerably more memory than a plain list, since it creates and links a separate node for shared prefix characters across many strings
options.feedback: Correct -- while shared prefixes are only stored once along a shared path, all the individual node objects and their many pointers can still add up to real overhead.

options.text: A trie always uses strictly less memory than any other way of storing the same set of strings
options.feedback: Tries can actually be memory-heavy due to their many linked nodes -- they don't universally guarantee the least memory usage.

options.text: A trie is physically incapable of storing more than 26 strings total
options.feedback: A trie's capacity isn't capped at 26 strings -- that number might describe branching per node for lowercase letters, not overall string capacity.

options.text: A trie requires every stored string to be exactly the same length
options.feedback: A trie can store strings of varying lengths without any such restriction.

easy.hard: Think about organizing words by their shared starting letters.
easy.medium: Words that begin the same way share the same early path through this structure.
easy.easy: It's a tree-shaped structure specifically organized around shared prefixes of stored strings.

medium.hard: Think about how quickly you could find every word that starts with, say, 'pre-'.
medium.medium: Because shared beginnings share the same path, everything reachable below a given point already starts the same way.
medium.easy: Walking down to a given prefix's node instantly narrows you down to only the words that begin with exactly that prefix.

hard.hard: Think about the cost of building a whole tree of individual letter-by-letter nodes and connections.
hard.medium: Even though shared prefixes are stored just once, the sheer number of separate node objects and pointers can add up.
hard.easy: Building this structure means creating and connecting a fresh node for every shared starting character across all the stored strings -- and that overhead can really pile up.

easy.text: What problem do self-balancing trees like AVL trees primarily solve?

options.text: They prevent a binary search tree from becoming lopsided and slow after many insertions or deletions
options.feedback: Correct -- a plain binary search tree can degrade into a slow, chain-like shape, and self-balancing trees actively correct for that.

options.text: They allow a tree to store data types that a regular tree cannot store
options.feedback: Self-balancing trees can generally store the same kinds of data as regular binary search trees -- the improvement is about SHAPE, not allowed data types.

options.text: They eliminate the need for a root node entirely
options.feedback: Self-balancing trees still have a root node, just like any other tree -- they don't remove that concept.

options.text: They make it impossible to ever delete a node once added
options.feedback: Self-balancing trees fully support deletion -- in fact, they specifically rebalance themselves after deletions too.

medium.text: In an AVL tree, what condition must hold true for the tree to remain 'balanced'?

options.text: For every node, the heights of its left and right subtrees differ by at most one
options.feedback: Correct -- this is the specific balance condition that gives AVL trees their name and guarantees fast operations.

options.text: Every node must have exactly two children, with none missing
options.feedback: AVL trees can have nodes with fewer than two children -- the balance condition is about subtree HEIGHT difference, not child count.

options.text: The tree must contain an even total number of nodes
options.feedback: An AVL tree's total node count can be odd or even -- balance is judged by subtree height difference at each node, not overall node count.

options.text: All values in the tree must be positive numbers
options.feedback: AVL trees can store negative values too -- the balance condition concerns subtree heights, not the sign of stored values.

hard.text: How does an AVL tree maintain its balance condition after an insertion or deletion that would otherwise violate it?

options.text: It performs one or more 'rotations' -- restructuring operations that rearrange a small number of nodes to restore the height-balance condition
options.feedback: Correct -- rotations are the mechanism AVL trees use to fix imbalance without giving up the underlying binary search tree ordering.

options.text: It deletes random nodes from the tree until the balance condition happens to be satisfied again
options.feedback: Randomly deleting nodes would lose data -- AVL trees instead use targeted rotations that preserve every stored value.

options.text: It simply ignores the imbalance and continues operating exactly as before
options.feedback: Ignoring the imbalance would defeat the purpose of a self-balancing tree -- AVL trees specifically detect and correct imbalance via rotations.

options.text: It rebuilds the entire tree completely from scratch after every single insertion or deletion
options.feedback: A full rebuild would be far more costly than necessary -- AVL trees use small, local rotations rather than starting over.

easy.easy: Think about what tends to go wrong with an ordinary binary search tree after many insertions in a bad order.
easy.medium: Without help, a plain binary search tree can end up shaped like a long lopsided chain instead of a bushy tree.
easy.hard: This kind of tree actively steps in to keep its shape close to balanced, avoiding the slow, chain-like degeneration a plain binary search tree can suffer.

medium.easy: Focus on comparing the heights of the two subtrees hanging off of any single node.
medium.medium: The rule caps how different the left and right subtree heights are allowed to be, at any given node.
medium.hard: Specifically, at every node, the left and right subtree heights can differ by no more than exactly one.

hard.easy: Think about a small, local restructuring move rather than starting over or deleting data.
hard.medium: This fix rearranges just a handful of nodes' connections, without discarding any of the stored values.
hard.hard: The move is called a rotation -- a targeted restructuring of a few nodes that restores the height-balance condition after it's been violated.

easy.text: What makes a 'circular' linked list different from a standard linked list?

options.text: The last node's pointer links back to the first node instead of pointing to nothing
options.feedback: Correct -- this circular connection is exactly what distinguishes it from a standard, non-circular linked list.

options.text: It can only store circular shapes as its data, such as circles or spheres
options.feedback: A circular linked list can store any kind of data -- 'circular' describes the shape of the LINKS, not the data type stored.

options.text: Every node in it must point to itself instead of to the next node
options.feedback: In a circular linked list, each node still points to the NEXT node in sequence -- it's only the very last node that loops back to the start.

options.text: It does not allow any new nodes to ever be added to it
options.feedback: New nodes can absolutely be added to a circular linked list, just as with any other linked list.

medium.text: What is one practical use case where a circular linked list is a natural fit?

options.text: Implementing a repeating cycle of items, such as players taking turns in a round-robin game
options.feedback: Correct -- since the last element links back to the first, the structure naturally supports endlessly cycling through a fixed group of items.

options.text: Storing values that must always remain in strictly descending numerical order
options.feedback: Maintaining strict descending numeric order isn't related to the circular connection -- that's a separate sorting concern.

options.text: Guaranteeing that a program can never enter an infinite loop
options.feedback: A circular linked list can actually make it easier to accidentally write an infinite loop if traversal isn't stopped carefully -- it doesn't prevent them.

options.text: Storing a single fixed value that can never be changed
options.feedback: A circular linked list is meant to store a sequence of multiple, changeable nodes, not just one unchangeable value.

hard.text: What extra care must be taken when writing code to traverse a circular linked list, compared to traversing a standard linked list?

options.text: The traversal must track a specific stopping condition (such as returning to the starting node), since there is no natural 'null' end to signal the list is finished
options.feedback: Correct -- without an explicit stopping condition, a naive traversal loop could run forever, since the 'next' pointer chain never reaches a natural end.

options.text: The traversal must convert every node's data into text before visiting it
options.feedback: There's no requirement to convert data to text -- the real added concern is detecting where to stop, since there's no natural ending point.

options.text: The traversal is required to visit nodes in strictly random order
options.feedback: Traversal order in a circular linked list still follows the pointer chain in sequence -- it isn't randomized.

options.text: The traversal can only be performed a single time for the entire lifetime of the list
options.feedback: A circular linked list can be traversed repeatedly, any number of times -- the key concern is just knowing when to stop each traversal.

easy.easy: The last node connects back to the first node, forming a loop rather than a dead-ending chain.
easy.medium: Instead of ending in a dead end, the very last node's pointer loops back around.
easy.hard: Think about what happens at the very last node's pointer -- does it point to nothing, or somewhere specific?

medium.easy: Because the last node loops back to the first, this structure is a natural fit for endlessly cycling through a fixed group, like turns in a game.
medium.medium: This structure fits situations where, after reaching the last item, you want to naturally continue right back to the first one again.
medium.hard: Think of a situation that naturally repeats over and over, cycling back to the start.

hard.easy: Because there's no natural dead end to signal 'stop', the traversal code has to explicitly track when it's arrived back at its starting node.
hard.medium: A standard linked list's final pointer naturally points to 'nothing,' but this structure's final pointer instead points right back to the start.
hard.hard: Think about what would normally tell you a linked list has ended, and whether that signal still exists here.

options.text: When two different keys are mapped by a hash function to the same storage slot
options.feedback: Correct -- a collision happens when the hash function assigns the same slot to more than one distinct key.

options.text: When a computer's hard drive physically crashes
options.feedback: A hash collision is a data-structure concept about two keys landing in the same slot, not a physical hardware failure.

options.text: When a program successfully finds the exact key it was searching for
options.feedback: Successfully finding a key is the desired, non-colliding outcome -- a collision refers to two DIFFERENT keys landing in the same slot.

options.text: When two entirely separate programs are run at the exact same time
options.feedback: Running two programs simultaneously is unrelated to hash collisions, which are specifically about keys mapping to the same storage slot.

medium.text: Why do hash collisions happen even with a well-designed hash function?

options.text: Because a hash function typically maps a much larger set of possible keys onto a smaller, fixed number of storage slots
options.feedback: Correct -- with more possible keys than available slots, some keys are mathematically guaranteed to share a slot eventually.

options.text: Because hash functions are required by definition to always produce the exact same output for every different input
options.feedback: A hash function producing identical output for every different input would make it useless -- collisions occur despite hash functions trying to spread keys out, not because they're forced to repeat one output.

options.text: Because hash tables are not allowed to store more than a single key at once
options.feedback: Hash tables are designed to store many keys -- collisions are about the mapping into slots, not a one-key limit.

options.text: Because computers cannot process more than one hashing operation per second
options.feedback: Processing speed has nothing to do with why collisions mathematically occur -- it's the mismatch between key-space size and slot count.

hard.text: What is 'chaining' as a strategy for handling hash collisions?

options.text: Each storage slot holds a small linked list (or similar structure) of all the keys that hashed to that same slot
options.feedback: Correct -- chaining resolves collisions by letting a slot hold multiple entries instead of just one.

options.text: The hash function is run repeatedly until it happens to stop producing any collisions at all
options.feedback: Chaining doesn't try to eliminate collisions by re-running the hash function -- it accepts that collisions happen and stores multiple entries per slot instead.

options.text: Colliding keys are simply discarded and never stored anywhere
options.feedback: Discarding data would lose information -- chaining specifically preserves every colliding key by linking them together at the same slot.

options.text: The entire hash table is resized to have exactly one slot per possible key in the universe
options.feedback: That would require an impractically enormous table -- chaining instead handles collisions locally, within the existing slot structure.

easy.hard: Think about two different pieces of data ending up assigned to the very same storage spot.
easy.medium: This happens when a mapping process assigns the same output slot to two different inputs.
easy.easy: It specifically describes two distinct keys being routed to the identical slot inside a hash-based structure.

medium.hard: Think about how many possible inputs there could be, versus how many storage slots actually exist.
medium.medium: There are usually far more possible keys than there are available slots to place them in.
medium.easy: Because the pool of possible keys vastly outnumbers the fixed number of available slots, some overlap becomes mathematically unavoidable eventually.

hard.hard: Think about letting a single storage slot hold more than one item instead of just one.
hard.medium: Rather than fighting collisions directly, this strategy just lets each slot hold a small list of everything that landed there.
hard.easy: Each slot ends up holding a small chain of entries, one for every key that happened to land there.

easy.text: What is a key advantage of a 'dynamic array' over a plain, fixed-size array?

options.text: A dynamic array can automatically grow to hold more elements than it originally had room for
options.feedback: Correct -- a dynamic array resizes itself as needed, unlike a fixed-size array whose capacity is set once and stays constant.

options.text: A dynamic array can never run out of available memory under any circumstances
options.feedback: A dynamic array can still eventually run into memory limits -- its advantage is flexible resizing, not unlimited memory.

options.text: A dynamic array always uses less total memory than a fixed-size array holding the same data
options.feedback: A dynamic array can actually use somewhat more memory due to reserved extra capacity -- its real advantage is the ability to grow, not guaranteed lower memory use.

options.text: A dynamic array cannot store more than a single data type
options.feedback: Whether an array can mix data types is a separate language feature, not what defines a 'dynamic' array -- the defining trait is its ability to resize.

medium.text: When a dynamic array runs out of room and needs to grow, what typically happens behind the scenes?

options.text: A new, larger block of memory is allocated, and the existing elements are copied over into it
options.feedback: Correct -- because the original memory block can't simply be extended in place, growth requires allocating a new block and copying existing data across.

options.text: The array's existing elements are permanently deleted to make room for new ones
options.feedback: Existing elements are preserved by copying them into the new, larger block -- they aren't deleted during a resize.

options.text: The computer's operating system is reinstalled to free up additional space
options.feedback: Reinstalling an operating system is unrelated to a dynamic array resizing -- resizing is a much smaller, routine memory operation.

options.text: The array converts itself into a linked list to gain more capacity
options.feedback: A dynamic array stays a dynamic array through a resize -- it doesn't transform into a different data structure like a linked list.

hard.text: Many dynamic array implementations double their capacity each time they need to grow, rather than growing by just one slot at a time. Why is this typically more efficient overall?

options.text: Doubling means resizing operations happen far less often, so the average (amortized) cost of adding an element stays low even though occasional resizes are individually expensive
options.feedback: Correct -- this is the idea behind 'amortized' constant-time appends: costly resizes happen rarely enough that their cost, spread out over many cheap appends, averages out to be small.

options.text: Doubling capacity guarantees that a resize will never be needed again for the rest of the program's lifetime
options.feedback: Even with doubling, further resizes can still eventually be needed as more elements keep being added -- it just makes resizes much less frequent, not eliminated entirely.

options.text: Doubling capacity is required in order for the array to support more than one data type
options.feedback: Supporting multiple data types is unrelated to the doubling growth strategy -- doubling is specifically about resize frequency and average cost.

options.text: Doubling capacity makes each individual element take up half as much memory
options.feedback: Doubling the array's overall capacity doesn't shrink the memory used per individual element -- the benefit is about how often costly resizes occur.

easy.easy: Think about what happens when a plain array is completely full and one more item needs to be added.
easy.medium: Unlike a fixed-size array, this structure can expand its own capacity automatically as needed.
easy.hard: The specific advantage is automatic growth in capacity, something a strictly fixed-size array cannot do on its own.

medium.easy: Since the surrounding memory might already be in use by something else, growing in place usually isn't possible.
medium.medium: Growth typically involves finding a fresh, bigger chunk of memory and moving everything over to it.
medium.hard: A new larger memory block gets allocated, and every existing element is copied over into that new block.

hard.easy: Think about how often a costly resize needs to happen if capacity grows by a lot each time, versus just a little.
hard.medium: Growing capacity aggressively means the expensive resize step happens rarely, even though each occurrence costs more.
hard.hard: Spreading a rare, expensive resize's cost out over many cheap appends is what keeps the AVERAGE cost per append low, even though any single resize is itself costly.

options.text: A conceptual description of a data structure's allowed operations and behavior, without specifying exactly how it's implemented
options.feedback: Correct -- an ADT defines WHAT operations are available and how they should behave, leaving the HOW up to a specific implementation.

options.text: A data type that a program is physically incapable of ever using
options.feedback: An abstract data type is fully usable in programs -- 'abstract' here refers to hiding implementation detail, not being unusable.

options.text: A synonym for the number data type specifically
options.feedback: An abstract data type is a general concept about behavior and operations, not a name specifically tied to numbers.

options.text: A data type that can only ever store a single, unchangeable value
options.feedback: An abstract data type can describe structures holding many values, like a whole stack or queue, not just one fixed unchangeable value.

medium.text: A 'stack' is often described as an abstract data type. What does that mean, specifically?

options.text: A stack is defined by the behavior of its operations (like push and pop) rather than by one single required underlying implementation
options.feedback: Correct -- a stack can be implemented using an array or a linked list underneath, as long as it honors the expected push/pop behavior.

options.text: A stack can only ever be implemented using a linked list, with no other implementation allowed
options.feedback: A stack's behavior can be implemented in more than one way, such as with an array OR a linked list -- that flexibility is exactly the point of calling it an ADT.

options.text: A stack must always be implemented directly in a computer's hardware circuitry
options.feedback: A stack is typically implemented in software, not hardware circuitry -- being an ADT is about behavior being implementation-independent, not about hardware.

options.text: A stack refers only to a physical, stacked pile of paper documents
options.feedback: In computer science, a 'stack' refers to the abstract behavior of last-in-first-out access, not literal paper documents.

hard.text: What is the practical benefit of programming against an abstract data type's interface (like 'enqueue' and 'dequeue' for a queue), rather than directly against one specific underlying implementation?

options.text: The underlying implementation can later be swapped out for a more efficient one without needing to rewrite the code that uses the ADT's operations
options.feedback: Correct -- this separation between defined behavior and implementation detail is a core reason abstract data types are useful in real software design.

options.text: It guarantees the program will run instantly, regardless of what implementation is chosen underneath
options.feedback: Performance still depends on the actual implementation chosen -- programming against an ADT's interface doesn't guarantee any particular speed.

options.text: It makes it impossible for the program to ever contain a bug
options.feedback: Using an ADT's interface doesn't eliminate bugs -- the real benefit is being able to change implementations without touching the code that just uses the defined operations.

options.text: It requires the programmer to rewrite the entire program every time the ADT is used
options.feedback: Programming against an ADT's interface actually reduces how much code needs to change later, rather than requiring a full rewrite every time it's used.

easy.easy: Think about describing WHAT something does, without pinning down exactly HOW it does it internally.
easy.medium: This concept focuses on defining allowed operations and expected behavior, leaving implementation details open.
easy.hard: There's a way of thinking about data that focuses on the outside view rather than anything happening under the hood.

medium.easy: Think about more than one possible way you could actually build the same expected behavior underneath.
medium.medium: The underlying implementation could be an array, or a linked list, or something else entirely, as long as the expected behavior holds.
medium.hard: What matters here isn't which building blocks are used, but whether the end result behaves the way it's supposed to.

hard.easy: Think about what stays the same for code using this concept, even if something changes deep underneath it.
hard.medium: Code that only relies on the defined operations doesn't need to change even if the underlying implementation is later replaced.
hard.hard: There's a reason changing what's running behind the scenes doesn't always mean rewriting everything that depends on it.
